name: Fatima Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Sunrise Foods, a neighbourhood supermarket with about twenty staff, in a residential area beside the old market square. I'm the senior on the bakery counter and the front tills. Mornings I bake off the bread, slice and bag it and then switch to the till when the lunchtime queue starts. By Friday I know half the street by name.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and do you use any AI tools yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is that it's a small place where the manager, Mr Pereira, actually asks my opinion. What wears me out is the early start at five thirty and the carrying, trays of rolls, boxes of flour. My shoulders tell me about it every Sunday. I use AI once in a while, mostly to scale up recipes and to write notes for the staff board. My boyfriend Tomás is an electrician, so he laughs that between us we cover the thinking and the wiring. We have a decent amount saved, about ten months of costs, and we rent a flat above a launderette.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a lot of noise. At work I'd tell the girls on the counter to keep doing what they're doing. To friends I'd say it's nice that nothing breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means very little. A chatbot isn't going to slice a loaf, and my job at Sunrise is fresh bread and people, with a bit of till work. I'd still be thinking about rent and Mr Pereira's worry that the discount chain across the road takes half his customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and my money plan, about five hundred a month into savings. I'd perhaps ask Mr Pereira if I could run a Saturday pastry special, because it sells. And I'd keep using the AI now and then for the recipe sums, since it's useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's an easy one, the sort where I get on with my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the discount chain. How worried are you about Sunrise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It's a small shop with small margins, and if it closed I'd find work but not as nice. Still, there are plenty of shops hiring and I've got savings, so I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the Saturday pastry special?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cinnamon buns and apple turnovers, from my grandmother's recipe. We sold out twice last winter when I tried it. I'd like to make it regular and ask for a bit extra pay for it.

say: I'd tell the girls on the counter to keep doing what they're doing.
I'd tell friends it's good that **nothing** breaks.
think: My job is fresh **bread** and people, which a chatbot can't do.
The discount chain across the road is my **real** worry for Sunrise.
do: Keep my shifts and put about five hundred a month into **savings**.
Ask Mr Pereira to make my Saturday **pastry** special regular.
S0.quote: A chatbot isn't going to slice a loaf, and my job at Sunrise is fresh bread and people, with a bit of till work.
fieldNote: Calm rests on secure hands-on work, ten months saved and plenty of nearby jobs.
She **worries** mildly about the shop itself and the discounter nearby, not about AI.

steps.text: Keep the bakery and front-till shifts at Sunrise
Put five hundred a month into savings
Ask Mr Pereira to make my Saturday pastry special regular

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change but we'll cope. At work I'd say whatever the head of the chain rolls out, let's try it in the shop and see if it works. Online I wouldn't say much, though I'd probably read a lot about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly a hands-on job, so less. They'd use it for ordering, the website, the app for coupons. I'd expect fewer people in head office and maybe a self-checkout lane or two added at Sunrise. The bakery is the part of the shop that survives best, because people like the smell and the person behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Pereira to let me learn the ordering system so I'm useful when the shop changes. I'd use the AI tools a bit more, for the weekly order estimates and stock forecasts. And I'd keep putting money aside, because change like this always costs somebody something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit uneasy at the edges. It's like watching the weather turn, you keep a coat in the bag.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a machine write your orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For flour and yeast, yes, if I could check it. For the bakery, I know what sells on a rainy Tuesday, and I'd want my judgment in the final say. It's help, not a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleagues would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Kapoor on the front tills. She's fifty-eight, she doesn't like the screens and she's been at Sunrise for twenty years. I'd teach her the new bits on my break if it came to that.

say: I'd say it's a big change but we'll **cope**, so let's try it in the shop.
I'd read a lot about it but say little **online**.
think: My job is mostly **hands-on**, so it hits me less.
The bakery should last longest because customers like the **smell** and the person.
do: Ask Mr Pereira to let me learn the **ordering** system.
Use AI for weekly order **estimates** and stock forecasts.
Keep putting money aside, as change always **costs** someone.
feel: **Fine**, with a bit of unease at the edges, like watching the weather turn.
S1.quote: The bakery is the part of the shop that survives best, because people like the smell and the person behind the counter.
fieldNote: She is calm here **because** her bakery and counter work is the part that lasts, and her partner's trade is secure.
She **worries** about Mrs Kapoor, a long-serving colleague, and offers to teach her on breaks.

steps.text: Learn the ordering system at Sunrise
Use AI for weekly flour and yeast estimates
Keep adding to savings each month
Teach Mrs Kapoor the new till screens on my breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and nobody should pretend otherwise. At work I'd gather the staff and say, let's talk to Mr Pereira about what Sunrise would do. Online I'd read, share a couple of things and hope someone in charge has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job's mostly physical, so I'd have until about 2031 for the robots, but the till part and the ordering go sooner. Even the bakery could be automated with bread machines. I'd be anxious because the chain would not wait for a small shop to be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, cut the extras and stretch our cushion to a year and a half. I'd learn a skill that stays human, perhaps pastry in a proper course, and sell at weekend markets. Tomás and I would think about him going self-employed, since electricians are in demand. And we'd delay the move to a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's scary but I'd do something every week, because that's how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pastry and the weekend market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People pay for something made by a person they can talk to, and a market stall is the opposite of a till. A stall costs about a hundred and fifty a week to run, and it could become a small business later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Tomás feel about being self-employed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's been talking about it for a year, so I think he'd be happy to be pushed. He'd do wiring, solar panels, charging points. That's the sort of work that grows if everything gets automated.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and nobody should pretend otherwise.
I'd gather the staff and ask Mr Pereira what **Sunrise** would do.
think: Even the bakery could be **automated** with bread machines in a few years.
A chain won't wait for a small shop to be **ready**.
do: Save harder and stretch the **cushion** to eighteen months.
Take a **pastry** course and sell at weekend markets.
Back **Tomás** going self-employed in wiring and charging points.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, doing something every week.
S2.quote: People pay for something made by a person they can talk to, and a market stall is the opposite of a till.
fieldNote: She is **anxious** because even her hands-on bakery job could be automated, yet her partner's trade gives her a base.
Her plan is **practical** and small, based on things she can already do.

steps.text: Run a weekend market stall selling buns and turnovers
Delay the move to a bigger flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to think about it properly. At work I'd tell colleagues to keep learning, and keep their savings healthy. To friends I'd say start now, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us it's still serious but more workable. The thinking AI part arrives by 2031 and the robots in 2034, so I'd have a few years where my own job isn't touched while the rest of the shop shifts around me. I'd be uneasy, and a bit more settled than in the first one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the pastry course this year and test a market stall on Saturdays. I'd save about five hundred a month and ask Mr Pereira about a senior counter manager role. I'd also use AI more, for pricing and planning, because if I'm going to run something myself I want help with the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly calm, but it sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mr Pereira about Sunrise's future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get ahead and make the shop a place people want to go, not just a place with cheap food. Fresh bread, a good counter and people who know names. The discount chain can't copy a shop where somebody knows your name and your usual loaf, though they'll try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still stay with Sunrise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, as long as it's alive. I like the people and I like being senior there. But I'd have the stall as a second leg, just in case.

say: I'd tell colleagues to keep learning and keep their **savings** healthy.
I'd tell friends to **start** now, not in year four.
think: My own job stays **untouched** for a few years while the shop shifts around me.
I'm uneasy but more **settled** than in the two-year case.
do: Start the **pastry** course and test a Saturday market stall.
Save about five hundred a month and ask about a **senior counter** role.
Use AI for **pricing** and planning my own sums.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly calm, but it sits there.
S3.quote: The discount chain can't copy a shop where somebody knows your name and your usual loaf, though they'll try.
fieldNote: Five years makes the **problem** workable, and she hedges by building a stall on the side while staying at Sunrise.
Her advice to her **manager** is about making the shop worth visiting.

steps.text: Start a pastry course this autumn
Use AI to price stall goods and plan weekly orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so be sensible and take it step by step. At work I'd say it's one more thing to keep an eye on. Online I'd forget to post at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I have time to build something of my own. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven and could be running the bakery, or my own shop, and robots in 2039 still feel far away. I'd probably have a child by then too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Sunrise, take the pastry course and gradually build up the market stall. I'd save for a deposit on a flat and put aside some for a business. I'd keep using AI now and then, it's a good helper, and I'd learn the new stuff when it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a long walk, and I like having time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own shop to be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like a small bakery cafe in a street like this one, with four tables, a good coffee machine and Tomás doing the wiring. It's the sort of place that you can't replace with a robot, because people go for the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a ten-year warning change when you have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, we'd still do it around thirty. But I'd make sure we had a proper emergency fund first and that one of us had secure work. Ten years means I can plan it properly.

say: I'd say ten years is long, so take it **step by step**.
I'd call it one more thing to **watch**, and forget to post.
think: Ten years gives me time to build something of my **own**.
Robots in **2039** still feel far away.
do: Carry on at Sunrise, finish the **pastry** course and grow the stall.
Save for a flat **deposit** and a small business fund.
Learn new AI tools when they are **proven**.
feel: **Calm**, like a long walk with plenty of time.
S4.quote: I'd like a small bakery cafe in a street like this one, with four tables, a good coffee machine and Tomás doing the wiring.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her turn a worry into a dream of a small bakery cafe, which fits her steady, **practical** manner.
Her calm comes from time, **savings** and a secure partner.

steps.text: Carry on at Sunrise while building the market stall
Grow the stall into regular weekend trade
Save a flat deposit and a small business fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Even a hands-on job like mine could be touched, and everyone would scramble at once. What would help is a warning from the big chains, and training that doesn't mean quitting my job. And small shops like Sunrise getting a chance, so they don't just close and leave us with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Nothing big. People talk about shops as if they're only tills and boxes, but a good one is somebody remembering your name and your usual loaf. I'd like the study to say that people like me think about how to keep that.

headlineQuote: People talk about shops as if they're only tills and boxes, but a good one is somebody remembering your name and your usual loaf.
portrait: **Fatima** is a 27-year-old senior on the bakery counter and front tills at Sunrise Foods, a small neighbourhood supermarket.
She is centre politically and steady, using **AI** now and then for recipes and notes.
Her boyfriend Tomás is an **electrician**, so the household has a hands-on income behind her.
She has about ten months saved, and her mood runs from calm to **anxious** when AGI is two years away.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** case, because even bakery work might be touched and everyone would scramble.
whatWouldHelp: A real **warning** from the big chains, training that doesn't mean quitting, and a chance for small shops.
